content.title: About
content.content: Enchilada, no meat is a classic Mexican dish made from corn or flour tortillas filled with vegetables, beans, cheese and spices, baked under a tomato or chili sauce. The dish is aromatic with coriander, cumin and paprika, offering a soft filling and a slightly crisp outer layer.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word enchilada comes from the Spanish “enchilar,” meaning “to coat with chili sauce.”
Traditionally the tortillas are made from masa (corn flour), but modern versions often use wheat flour.
The vegetarian version gained popularity in the US in the 1970s as part of the health‑food movement.
There are many regional sauce variations, from green salsa verde to red salsa roja.
Enchiladas are commonly served with rice, beans and guacamole on the side.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Beans and cheese provide essential amino acids that support muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables and beans aid digestion and help regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tortillas and beans contain thiamine, niacin and folate, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from the sauce
items.content: Tomatoes and chili peppers are rich in lycopene and vitamin C, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The absence of meat and moderate cheese amount make the dish heart‑friendly.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese in the filling can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces often contain high salt levels; low‑sodium options are recommended.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Cheese and oil can make the dish calorie‑rich, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Spicy ingredients
items.content: Chili may irritate the stomach of individuals with sensitive digestive systems.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve enchiladas hot, topped with extra sauce and grated cheese. Add a dollop of sour cream, guacamole or fresh cilantro if desired. For a lighter version, use whole‑grain tortillas and reduce the cheese amount.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked enchiladas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For freezing, place them in a zip‑lock bag and keep for 2‑3 months. Reheat until the internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

frankfurters-or-hot-dogs-with-tomato-bas.title: Frankfurters or hot dogs with tomato-based sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Frankfurters or hot dogs served in a flavorful tomato‑based sauce are a ready‑to‑eat meat product. The sauce typically contains tomatoes, onion, spices and a touch of sugar, giving it a sweet‑tart taste. The product is often sold in single‑serve packs that can be heated in a microwave or on the stovetop.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tomato sauce is frequently enriched with paprika and oregano for a brighter flavor.
Frankfurters originated in Germany but are now mass‑produced worldwide, including the United States and Russia.
Tomatoes used in the sauce may be fresh or canned, simplifying manufacturing.
The product is common in children’s menus because it cooks quickly and has a soft texture.
Some recipes add a small amount of vinegar to the sauce to boost acidity.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The sausages provide animal protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat in the product is rich in vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes supply lycopene, an antioxidant that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Meat contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Convenient and quick
items.content: A ready‑to‑heat meal saves time while delivering a satisfying portion of nutrients.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Both the sauce and the sausages often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Meat products can contain saturated fats that, in excess, increase cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Preservatives and flavor enhancers
items.content: To extend shelf life, nitrites, phosphates and artificial flavors may be added.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to components of the sausages.

items.title: Added sugar in the sauce
items.content: Tomato sauce is often sweetened, raising the overall calorie count.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the package in the microwave (2–3 minutes) or in a skillet, stirring so the sauce coats the sausages evenly. Serve with bread, mashed potatoes, rice or a vegetable salad. Optional toppings include grated cheese or fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unopened packs in a cool, dry place at 0 °C to +25 °C. Once opened, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator and consume within 3‑4 days. Discard if the product develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

frozen-mocha-coffee-drink-with-non-dairy.title: Frozen mocha coffee drink with non-dairy milk and whipped cream

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen mocha coffee drink is a refreshing frozen beverage made from cold coffee, chocolate syrup, non-dairy milk (such as oat or almond) and a thick layer of non-dairy whipped cream. Served as a soft‑serve ice cream, it combines the aromatic coffee flavor, sweet chocolate notes and a creamy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frozen coffee drinks first appeared in the United States in the 1990s as an alternative to traditional ice cream.
Mocha blends coffee and chocolate flavors, making it a favorite among dessert‑drink lovers.
Plant‑based milks allow people with lactose intolerance or vegans to enjoy the drink without compromising taste.
Non‑dairy whipped cream is often made from coconut cream, adding a subtle tropical hint.
Freezing coffee retains most of its caffeine, so the drink can still provide a stimulating effect.

items.title: Caffeine boost
items.content: Caffeine improves alertness and can increase energy levels, especially useful on hot days.

items.title: Antioxidants from cocoa
items.content: Chocolate syrup contains flavonoids that may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Low lactose content
items.content: Using non‑dairy milk makes the drink safe for those with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Vitamins from plant milk
items.content: Oat, almond or soy milks are often fortified with vitamin D and calcium.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: If whole coffee grounds or oat flakes are added, the drink can provide soluble fiber.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: High caffeine intake may cause anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Chocolate syrup and whipped cream usually contain added sugars, increasing calorie count.

items.title: Nut allergies
items.content: Plant‑based milks derived from nuts can trigger allergic reactions in susceptible people.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A frozen drink with whipped cream can be high in calories; moderate consumption is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the frozen mocha coffee drink in a glass or cup, top with an extra swirl of whipped cream and dust with cocoa powder or grated chocolate. A pinch of cinnamon or sea salt can add a pleasant contrast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen beverage in an airtight container in the freezer at –18 °C. Over time ice crystals may form; let the drink sit 5‑10 minutes at room temperature before serving to soften.

content.title: About
content.content: Okra is the edible pod of the plant Abelmoschus esculentus, native to tropical and subtropical regions. The pods have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a crisp texture. Okra is commonly prepared steamed, boiled, or cooked without added fat, and is used in soups, stews, and stir‑fries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Okra is also known as "lady's finger" or "gumbo" in different cuisines.
The mucilaginous substance in the pods helps thicken soups and sauces.
In Africa and Southeast Asia okra is used in traditional medicine to aid digestion.
Okra seeds are rich in oil that is sometimes pressed for cosmetic products.
Okra can be grown in containers, making it popular among urban gardeners.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber in okra supports healthy bowel function and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low‑calorie plant protein
items.content: The pods provide plant‑based protein that helps maintain muscle mass with modest calorie intake.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Okra supplies thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2) and niacin (B3), which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in okra help neutralize free radicals and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports blood sugar balance
items.content: The mucilage slows carbohydrate absorption, which may contribute to more stable glycemic responses.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to okra, ranging from skin rash to swelling.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Raw pods contain small amounts of oxalates that can cause gastrointestinal discomfort if consumed in excess.

items.title: Digestive sensitivity
items.content: The high mucilage content may cause bloating or gas in people with sensitive stomachs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Okra can be steamed, boiled, sautéed, or quickly stir‑fried without added fat. Pods are often added to soups, stews, vegetable mixes, and salads. Before cooking, slice and rinse the pods to reduce excess slime.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh okra in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or container to retain moisture for 3‑5 days. For longer storage, blanch the pods for 2‑3 minutes and freeze them.

content.title: About
content.content: Pretzel chips are crunchy slices of dough shaped like traditional pretzels and baked until they become hard. They are completely gluten‑free, making them suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity. The flavor is mildly salty with a toasted‑dough aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hard pretzel chips originated in the United States as a gluten‑free alternative to regular potato chips.
Their firm texture is achieved by a double‑bake at low temperature.
The gluten‑free version is made from a blend of rice, corn, and potato flours.
Chips are often seasoned with paprika, garlic, cheese, or dill.
They are popular among athletes as a light source of quick‑release carbohydrates.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many snack foods, these chips contain a modest amount of fat, making them a lighter option.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Starch from rice and corn flour releases energy slowly, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Fully safe for individuals with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Contains small amounts of B‑vitamins
items.content: The whole‑grain base provides thiamine (B1) and niacin (B3), which support metabolism.

items.title: Crunch promotes satiety
items.content: The hard texture stimulates chewing receptors, helping you feel full longer.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Chips are often salted; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Corn or rice allergy
items.content: Ingredients may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Large servings can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: The hard texture makes them unsuitable for young children without supervision.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pretzel chips can be enjoyed straight from the bag, added to salads, soups, or used as a crunchy base for dip‑laden dishes. They are convenient for on‑the‑go snacking in a sealed package.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep chips in an airtight bag in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store them in the refrigerator to preserve crunch. Discard any chips that become soft or develop an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Greek yogurt without added sugar is made from whole cow's milk that undergoes double straining, resulting in a thick, creamy texture. Unlike fruit‑flavored versions, it has a neutral taste, making it versatile for cooking and as a base for sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Greek yogurt contains two to three times more protein than regular yogurt.
The lack of added sugar makes it suitable for low‑carb diets.
Traditionally in Greece it was made from sheep's milk, but most modern products use cow's milk.
Its thick texture is often used as a substitute for sour cream in dips and sauces.
Opened Greek yogurt can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks if tightly sealed.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: One cup (200 ml) of Greek yogurt provides about 20 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: Live cultures such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low sugar
items.content: No added sugar helps control blood glucose levels.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Calcium strengthens bones and teeth and is essential for muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yogurt supplies vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Although some lactose is removed during straining, the product still contains lactose and may cause discomfort for sensitive individuals.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Casein and whey proteins can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High fat in full‑fat versions
items.content: Full‑fat Greek yogurt can be calorie‑dense; choose low‑fat options for weight‑management goals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Plain Greek yogurt without sugar works well as a base for smoothies, sauces, dips, and as a sour‑cream substitute in baking. Pair it with nuts, seeds, vegetables, or use it in marinades for meat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the yogurt in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C in its original container. After opening, keep the lid tightly closed. Discard if it develops off‑odors, mold, or an unusual texture.
